categories.name: Mammals
categories.description: Mammals use the Amazon's forests, rivers, and wetlands in many different ways.

animals.name: Jaguar
animals.summary: A powerful rainforest cat that helps regulate prey populations.

image.alt: Black jaguar resting on a log
image.credit: Photo: Cburnett via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

animals.habitat: Dense forests, wetlands, river edges, and seasonally flooded areas.
animals.diet: An opportunistic carnivore that can take fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals.
animals.behavior: Usually solitary. Jaguars are strong swimmers and often travel along rivers.
animals.range: The Amazon Basin is one of the most important strongholds for the species.
animals.conservation: Main conservation concerns include habitat loss, fragmentation, conflict with people, and loss of prey.
quickFacts: Jaguars are the largest cats in the Americas.
They have an exceptionally powerful bite.
Their rosettes often contain small spots in the center.

animals.name: Southern Two-toed Sloth
animals.summary: A slow-moving tree dweller that spends much of its life in the canopy.
animals.habitat: Lowland and flooded tropical forests, especially areas with abundant trees.
animals.diet: Mostly leaves, flowers, and other plant material.
animals.behavior: Arboreal and generally solitary. It is more active at night and can swim when needed.
animals.range: Found across much of northern South America, including large areas of the Amazon.
animals.conservation: Forest protection is important because sloths depend on connected tropical habitat.
quickFacts: Two-toed sloths have long curved claws.
Their slow metabolism helps conserve energy.
Algae can grow in their coarse fur, helping them blend into vegetation.

animals.name: Giant River Otter
animals.summary: A social aquatic mammal adapted to rivers, lakes, and slow-moving waterways.

image.credit: Photo: Charles J. Sharp via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

animals.habitat: Freshwater rivers, oxbow lakes, flooded forests, and wetlands.
animals.diet: Mostly fish, with crustaceans and other aquatic prey also taken.
animals.behavior: Highly social. Families cooperate while traveling, hunting, and raising pups.
animals.range: Occurs in parts of the Amazon, Orinoco, and La Plata river systems.
animals.conservation: Pollution, habitat loss, overfishing, and historical hunting have affected populations.
quickFacts: Giant river otters can form family groups.
They use vocalizations to communicate.
They are strong swimmers with streamlined bodies.

animals.name: Capybara
animals.summary: The world's largest living rodent, closely tied to freshwater habitats.

image.credit: Photo: Dick Culbert from Gibsons, B.C., Canada via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

animals.habitat: Riverbanks, wetlands, flooded forests, and grassy areas near water.
animals.diet: Grasses, aquatic plants, and other vegetation.
animals.behavior: Social and semi-aquatic. Groups often rest near water and use swimming to escape danger.
animals.range: Widely distributed across northern and central South America.
animals.conservation: They are relatively adaptable, but healthy wetlands and freshwater systems remain important.
quickFacts: Capybaras can remain underwater for several minutes.
They commonly live in groups.
Their feet are partly webbed.

categories.name: Birds
categories.description: The Amazon supports an enormous variety of birds, from canopy specialists to riverside species.

animals.name: Harpy Eagle
animals.summary: A large forest raptor with powerful talons adapted for hunting in the canopy.

image.alt: Harpy eagle moving through rainforest vegetation
image.credit: Photo: Haui Ared via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

animals.habitat: Mature tropical forests with tall trees suitable for nesting.
animals.diet: Mostly arboreal mammals and large birds.
animals.behavior: Uses powerful flight and surprise attacks to hunt among trees.
animals.range: The species occurs through parts of Central and South America, including the Amazon.
animals.conservation: Large areas of mature forest are important for nesting and hunting.
quickFacts: Harpy eagles have extremely strong feet and talons.
They build large nests high in trees.
They are among the largest living eagles.

animals.name: Scarlet Macaw
animals.summary: A brightly colored parrot known for strong social bonds and loud calls.

image.alt: Two scarlet macaws on a branch
image.credit: Photo: Cburnett via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

animals.habitat: Lowland rainforest, forest edges, and river corridors.
animals.diet: Fruit, seeds, nuts, and other plant material.
animals.behavior: Social and highly vocal, often traveling in pairs or small groups.
animals.range: Found from southern Mexico through much of northern South America.
animals.conservation: Habitat loss and capture for the wildlife trade are major concerns in parts of their range.
quickFacts: Scarlet macaws have strong curved bills.
They can live for decades.
Pairs often remain closely bonded.

animals.name: Toco Toucan
animals.summary: A large toucan recognized by its oversized colorful bill.

image.alt: Toco toucan perched on a branch
image.credit: Photo: Ankit Kadam via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

animals.habitat: Forest edges, riverine woodland, savanna-forest mosaics, and tropical forests.
animals.diet: Fruit is important, along with insects, eggs, and small animals.
animals.behavior: Moves through the canopy and uses its bill to reach food.
animals.range: Broadly distributed in South America, including parts of the Amazon Basin.
animals.conservation: Maintaining forest and tree-cavity habitat supports breeding populations.
quickFacts: The bill is large but relatively light because of its internal structure.
Toco toucans are strong fliers despite their bulky appearance.
They swallow fruit whole.

animals.name: Hoatzin
animals.summary: A leaf-eating bird strongly associated with riverside and seasonally flooded vegetation.

image.credit: Photo: Philipp Hoenle, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

animals.habitat: Wet forests, swamps, and vegetation along slow-moving rivers and lagoons.
animals.diet: Mostly leaves, with some flowers and fruits.
animals.behavior: Often rests in groups near water. Young birds can use clawed wing digits to move through vegetation.
animals.range: Occurs across parts of the northern and central Amazon Basin and adjacent tropical South America.
animals.conservation: Protection of wetlands and riverside vegetation helps preserve suitable habitat.
quickFacts: Hoatzins have a specialized digestive system for fermenting leaves.
They are poor fliers compared with many other birds.
Young birds have temporary claws on their wings.

categories.name: Reptiles
categories.description: Reptiles occupy the forest floor, waterways, and canopy.

animals.name: Green Anaconda
animals.summary: A huge semi-aquatic constrictor that spends much of its time in and around water.

image.credit: Photo: Steven G. Johnson via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

animals.habitat: Swamps, marshes, flooded forests, slow rivers, and oxbow lakes.
animals.diet: Fish, birds, turtles, and a variety of mammals.
animals.behavior: Usually ambushes prey from water and constricts it before swallowing.
animals.range: Found across much of tropical northern South America.
animals.conservation: Wetland and river protection helps maintain their habitat and prey base.
quickFacts: Green anacondas are excellent swimmers.
Females are much larger than males.
Their eyes and nostrils are positioned high on the head.

animals.name: Black Caiman
animals.summary: A large crocodilian that occupies rivers, floodplains, and other freshwater habitats.

image.alt: Black caiman, Rupununi River in southwestern Guyana
image.credit: Photo: David Stanley via Wikimedia Commons.

animals.habitat: Slow rivers, lagoons, flooded forests, and wetlands.
animals.diet: Fish, birds, reptiles, and mammals, with prey varying by age.
animals.behavior: Often waits motionless near the water's edge and becomes more active after dark.
animals.range: Native to much of the Amazon Basin.
animals.conservation: Wetland protection and sustainable management of wildlife are important to recovery and long-term survival.
quickFacts: Black caimans are among the largest caimans.
Young animals eat smaller prey than adults.
They play an important role as freshwater predators.

animals.name: Green Iguana
animals.summary: A tree-dwelling lizard commonly associated with warm tropical forests and rivers.

image.alt: Green iguana (Iguana iguana), the Pantanal, Brazil
image.credit: Photo: Charles J. Sharp via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

animals.habitat: Forest edges, riverbanks, and trees close to water.
animals.diet: Mostly leaves, shoots, flowers, and fruit.
animals.behavior: Basks in warm areas and can dive or swim to escape predators.
animals.range: Occurs widely through tropical Central and South America.
animals.conservation: Forest and riparian habitat protection helps populations remain stable.
quickFacts: Green iguanas are strong swimmers.
They use a long tail for balance and defense.
Juveniles often spend more time on lower vegetation.

animals.name: Red-footed Tortoise
animals.summary: A land tortoise recognized by the reddish scales on its legs and head.

image.credit: Photo: Flints via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

animals.habitat: Forest, savanna, and forest-edge environments with access to cover and food.
animals.diet: A broad plant-based diet including leaves, fruits, flowers, and fallen vegetation.
animals.behavior: Mostly terrestrial and active during warm, humid periods.
animals.range: Occurs in northern and central South America, including the Amazon region.
animals.conservation: Habitat conversion and illegal collection can affect populations.
quickFacts: The shell can show yellow, orange, or red markings.
Red-footed tortoises use scent and visual cues to communicate.
They can live for many decades.

categories.name: Amphibians
categories.description: Warm, humid forests and clean water create important habitat for frogs and other amphibians.

animals.name: Poison Dart Frog
animals.summary: A group of colorful frogs famous for chemical defenses and rainforest lifestyles.

image.alt: Red poison dart frog on forest litter
image.credit: Photo: Dwayne Reilander via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

animals.habitat: Moist tropical forests, leaf litter, and vegetation near streams.
animals.diet: Mostly very small insects and other invertebrates.
animals.behavior: Many species are active by day and use bright colors as warning signals.
animals.range: Dart frog species occur across tropical Central and South America; several occur in Amazonian and neighboring forests.
animals.conservation: Protecting clean, humid forest habitat is essential because amphibians are sensitive to environmental change.
quickFacts: Not every poison dart frog is highly toxic in the wild.
Diet can influence the chemicals present in some species.
Many species care for their eggs and tadpoles.

animals.name: Glass Frog
animals.summary: Small tree frogs known for translucent skin and a life closely connected to streams.

image.alt: Glass frog viewed from the side
image.credit: Photo: Mauricio Rivera Correa via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5.

animals.habitat: Humid forests near clear streams and small rivers.
animals.diet: Small insects and other tiny invertebrates.
animals.behavior: Mostly nocturnal and often found on leaves above flowing water.
animals.range: Glass frogs are diverse across tropical Central and South America, including the Amazon region.
animals.conservation: Clean streams and intact forest are important for their reproductive cycle.
quickFacts: Some species have translucent skin through which organs can be seen.
Eggs are commonly laid on vegetation above streams.
Tadpoles drop into the water after hatching.

animals.name: Amazon Horned Frog
animals.summary: A large, broad-bodied frog that uses camouflage and ambush tactics.

image.credit: Photo: Maarten Sepp via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

animals.habitat: Humid lowland rainforest and moist leaf litter.
animals.diet: Insects and other small animals; larger individuals can take substantial prey.
animals.behavior: Often remains buried in leaf litter and waits for prey to approach.
animals.range: Found in parts of the western and central Amazon region.
animals.conservation: Forest and leaf-litter habitat protection is important.
quickFacts: Its horn-like projections help break up the outline of the head.
It has a very wide mouth for an amphibian.
Camouflage is a major part of its hunting strategy.

animals.name: Red-eyed Tree Frog
animals.summary: A bright green tree frog with vivid eyes and strong climbing ability.

image.credit: Photo: Careyjamesbalboa (Carey James Balboa) via Wikimedia Commons.

animals.habitat: Lowland tropical forests and vegetation near ponds or streams.
animals.diet: Mostly insects and other small invertebrates.
animals.behavior: Nocturnal and arboreal. It uses sticky toe pads to cling to leaves.
animals.range: Native to parts of Central America and northern South America.
animals.conservation: Forest loss and changes to breeding habitat can affect local populations.
quickFacts: The large eyes may help startle predators.
Its toe pads help it climb smooth vegetation.
Breeding often occurs around temporary or permanent water.
